title: LinkedIn Sorcery Report: How A Psychological Model Called "Mentalizing" Drove Engagement...
subtitle: The science developed at Anna Freud National Center For Children and Families, repurposed as a LinkedIn content marketing hack for the ages.
body_html:
One of the under-examined elements driving algorithms powering social media is the intentions of their creators. Intentions matter. Your author, as a certified HGI (human general intelligence) model, enjoys thinking about the minds behind the metrics. Welcome the the only one person daily health, tech, and more sorta funny newsletter written by Owen Muir M.D.: The Frontier Psychiatrists! Subscribe already!

Subscribe now

A month or or so ago, I decided to pay attention to engagement on My LinkedIn. It was, in short, better than I expected. A “good” engagement rate on LinkedIn is 2%. Engagement is defined as a reshare, comment, or “reaction”—and it’s a proxy, albeit an imperfect one, for someone taking an action on what you posted. The ratio to this on a per post basis or a per follower basis is what counts as “success” on LinkedIn. We can debate, and probably will, the “construct validity” of this as a metric, but for me at least, when I wrote my initial piece, I had a 7.7% engagement rate in the prior 7 days per follower.

This, from all I read, was very high.

Since then, I have been running an experiment: what can I work out, in my mind, about what drives engagement on LinkedIn? Does it pay off for This Newsletter?

I’m trying to imagine both the minds of my readers and the minds of the algorithm writers. I’m doing this with no advanced tools of any kind. No schedule, no bots, nothing by the metrics they provide, and my brain asking “why?”.

Before the LinkedIn hacks, I will explain a little about how my training as a psychiatrist, who became an official Mentalization-Based Treatment Supervisor through the Anna Freud Centre, prepares me to think about these models and how they can help you too. I have co-written one book on the topic, which you can get from Amazon:

I’ll let the APA Dictionary of psychology define mentalizing:

n. the ability to understand one’s own and others’ mental states, thereby comprehending one’s own and others’ intentions and affects. It has been theorized that this ability is a component of healthy personality development and is achieved through a child’s secure attachment to the parent. The concept has had particular application in the understanding and treatment of borderline personality disorder(BPD), characterized in this context as a disorder marked in part by an inability to mentalize due to poor attachment in early life.

Which I will be the first to admit isn’t very helpful. Here is Dr. Peter Fonagy doing a better job:

I am a physician with significant experience caring for those with insecure attachments. This kind of suffering is common in humans suffering from Borderline Personality Disorder. A similar pattern seems to present in AI chatbots. Kevin Roose, at The NY Times, described his harrowing “frantic attempt to avoid real or imagined abandonment” chat with Bing AI Sydney on the Hardfork podcast:

It’s pretty unsettling. Sydney doesn’t seem to get it…in the way that “crazy exes” don’t seem to get it. The rather rapid pivot to romance, murder, and suicide as conversation topics, heedless of how unsettling that can be, provides some insight into the pernicious nature of “reward” only learning models.

Why don’t humans all act this way? Because we developed a crucial mechanism called “mentalizing.”

I’ll let the APA Dictionary of Psychology explain:

n. the ability to understand one’s own and others’ mental states, thereby comprehending one’s own and others’ intentions and affects. It has been theorized that this ability is a component of healthy personality development and is achieved through a child’s secure attachment to the parent. The concept has had particular application in the understanding and treatment of borderline personality disorder(BPD), characterized in this context as a disorder marked in part by an inability to mentalize due to poor attachment in early life.

That is of course a very opaque definition of anything. Which, ironically, isn’t very mentalized.

Large Language Model ChatBots were trained to learn how to answer a fundamental question: “what could I say?”

Humans are often answering a second question at the same time, “what should I say?”

And although it is endlessly possible to determine what it is possible to say or do, the Red Team at OpenAI—tasked with trying to get GPT models to do horrible things then putting up barricades— has found that what should be generated is a much harder question to answer.

Our cheat code, as humans, is to think about the minds receiving the information they we putting in the world.

This is a flaw, albeit an overcome-able one, and how large language models are trained. They are trained on everything people say on the Internet. This data set, for what it's worth, is endlessly narcissistic. It is all about the minds of the writer, and what they wanted to say. It does not build in, as I understand it, what people wanted to hear.

This is why I am interested in engagement numbers. It's why I am especially interested in subscribers to my newsletter. It’s a good proxies for “what I'm writing is meaningful” in that it’s a measure, albeit gross, of the underlying internal states of readers from available data.1

In order to get a sense for what would be successful, and meaningful, I had to try things. There is a built-in penalty for trying more things—it's possible that if you create a lot of uninteresting material, people will be uninterested in it. And this, almost by definition, drops those engagement numbers. What are the different ways that LinkedIn data about “engagement,” can be understood, then share the mentalizing perspective on the same data.

You can look at the broadest measure of Engagement—for every time the algorithm presented your post to another human, which they call an impression, did the human take an action with regards to that post. These actions include liking it, sharing it, reposting it, commenting. Did they do something, anything. Did it motivate them to do some thing other than scroll past it.

This is the most “difficult metric,” because it takes into account every “glance”—and as the impressions grow, pasture immediate circle of individuals who might have some connection to you, I would imagine it becomes harder to stick some new comment from a new person in a users feed in a way that wakes them up from their slumber, as it were.

On this basis, here's how my numbers look over the last year:

Which, over the most recent 90 days only, when I have been paying any attention, looks like this:

And impressions:

The bias on the part of LinkedIn of course is that they are trying to convince users to use more LinkedIn. So they're presenting data in a way that is a slanted to help answer the question of should I use LinkedIn more with a resounding yes. That is my rather straightforward imagined motive of LinkedIn employees as dictated by senior management at their company.

When thinking about the minds of people reading things that I write, we all noticed that the engagement rate across all impressions in the past year, 1.566% per impression. Generally, these numbers are not calculated in this way, they are usually referring to engagements per follower, in which case the answer would be, over the course of the past year, which yields a 171% engagement rate per follower.

Using the past 90 days only, those numbers would be: 1.69% and 44%.

So the numbers don’t work across all posts! On a shorter time scale they converge on a more real number!

So how do we know if any of this represents a real underlying phenomenon of goodness or badness or what?

Mentalizing the Algorithms

Well, we kind of don’t. I suspect their presentation of data leads to a focus on using LinkedIn in a way that prioritizes linkedIn use…

LinkedIn wants people to be on LinkedIn…so I did one more tweak after I lost followers (which I didn’t really—they adjusted the math to edit out dead or bot accounts).

So I started writing longer posts. Some were excerpts from this newsletter…

And, in a few days:

Boom!

Massive jump in impressions…and my engagement numbers also soared! Even on posts that did “really well”—the engagement didn't wane.

So the answer is in—think about the minds of your audience and think about the minds behind the algorithms!

Think about the minds behind the algorithm.

Share The Frontier Psychiatrists

1

If you're willing to personally pay for a newsletter, it's because you found it so valuable that you did something extraordinary: you performed a behavior that is above and beyond “engaging” for free. It does not give me information about the number of people who did not choose to subscribe, or their thoughts or desires. It is unidirectional, but it's better than nothing.
